analysis.one_liner: Let employers offer time off instead of cash overtime and loosen overtime scheduling rules.
analysis.headline: The Senate fell short twice on votes to cut off debate — 53-47 and then 51-47 against the 60 needed — so the bill never got a final vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let private employers offer workers one-and-a-half hours of paid time off instead of cash overtime, let them schedule up to 80 hours across two weeks without paying overtime in the heavier week, and made it harder for workers to challenge "exempt" classifications that carry no overtime rights. Participation would have been voluntary, union contracts honored, and unused comp time paid out in cash by January 31 of the following year.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers of hourly workers gain the most: they could substitute time off for overtime cash, hold unused comp time on their books until the following January, run 50-hour weeks without an overtime premium as long as the two-week total stayed at 80 hours, and face fewer court challenges over salaried-exempt classifications. A minority of workers who genuinely prefer time off to extra pay would gain an option federal employees have had since 1978.

how_it_helps.text: Lets employers pay overtime in time-and-a-half time off instead of cash, with unused comp time cashed out no sooner than January 31 of the following year — an interest-free deferral of overtime wages to the employer.

Lets employers establish biweekly schedules of up to 80 hours over two weeks, so a 50-hour week carries no overtime premium if the next week is light — moving the overtime trigger off the 40-hour week.

Bars courts from counting sub-full-day pay deductions or overtime add-ons when deciding whether a 'salaried' employee is exempt from overtime, making it easier for employers to keep that status and harder for workers to challenge it.

Gives workers who prefer time off an option similar to federal employees', with voluntary signup, anti-coercion rules, employer payouts on request or at termination, and collective bargaining agreements honored.

analysis.who_pays: Hourly workers whose overtime could be paid in time off rather than cash: the employer decides when the time can be used, unused hours can sit for up to a year before cash-out, and workers with fluctuating schedules could lose the overtime premium in heavy weeks. Workers whose 'exempt' status is challenged would find the challenge harder to win.

drawbacks.text: The employer, not the worker, controls when comp time can be used: the bill only requires the employer to allow its use 'within a reasonable period' if it does not 'unduly disrupt' operations, so time off can be deferred indefinitely in busy workplaces.
Under biweekly programs, a worker could put in 50 hours one week and receive no overtime premium at all, as long as the two-week total stayed at or under 80 hours.
Unused comp time could sit on the employer's books for up to a year before mandatory cash-out on January 31, effectively lending the worker's overtime wages to the employer.
The exempt-status provision shields pay-deduction practices from being used as evidence in overtime lawsuits, weakening the main tool workers had to challenge bogus 'salaried' classifications.
Even supporters concede that in non-union workplaces the 'voluntary' agreement may not feel voluntary, since the employer writes the terms and the worker's job depends on staying agreeable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The flexibility is real — federal employees have used comp time, biweekly schedules, and credit hours since 1978, and this bill copied those rules with voluntary participation, anti-coercion penalties, and cash-out rights. But the federal analogy flatters the private-sector version: a government agency is not trying to minimize a payroll, while a private employer deciding when comp time can be used, holding accrued wages up to a year, and gaining a diluted 40-hour overtime trigger holds all the leverage. The two provisions unrelated to comp time — biweekly scheduling and the exempt-status change — have no family-friendly purpose at all and shift money and legal risk from employers to workers. On balance the bill offered modest, real options for some workers at a substantial cost to the cash-overtime guarantee that protects all of them.

outcome.mechanism: Two Senate votes to cut off debate failed at 53-47 and 51-47, short of the 60 needed, so the bill never got an up-or-down final vote and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator John Ashcroft introduced the bill on January 21, 1997 with a list of Republican co-sponsors; it ultimately drew 42 Republican co-sponsors and none from the other party.

The Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, chaired by Senator James Jeffords, held subcommittee hearings in February, marked the bill up in March, and reported it favorably with an amendment on April 2, 1997, with minority views filed; it was placed on the Senate calendar.

The Senate took the bill up in May 1997, but a vote to cut off debate on the modified committee amendment — a procedure needing 60 senators — failed 53-47 on May 15, with all 45 Democrats voting no and 53 of 55 Republicans voting yes.
Supporters tried again three weeks later; the second debate-ending vote failed 51-47 on June 4, 1997, again with zero Democrats in favor and 51 of 55 Republicans in favor.
With no way past the 60-vote threshold, the bill never received a final Senate vote, never reached the House, and expired when the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hourly workers kept the guaranteed right to cash overtime and the 40-hour trigger that protects it, and the employer groups seeking comp-time flexibility and exemption from overtime lawsuits gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hourly workers who kept cash overtime

sides.party_line_note: The vote to cut off debate split almost entirely by party: every Democrat present voted no both times (45-0 and 44-0), while 53 and then 51 of 55 Republicans voted yes, with only 2 and 3 Republicans defecting.

industries.industry: Employers of hourly workers (retail, restaurants, health care, manufacturing)
industries.note: The bill would have let these employers substitute comp time for cash overtime, defer cashing out unused time to the following January, run 80-hour biweekly schedules without weekly overtime premiums, and face fewer lawsuits over 'exempt' classifications. Each of those gains comes directly out of workers' control over their overtime pay and schedules.

Union contracts would have been honored, but the bill would have extended comp-time substitution into the largely non-union workplaces where most hourly workers are, eroding the cash-overtime standard unions defend. Unions opposed the bill, and the committee's minority filed views against it.
